title: A Number Written Down and Read Back: Why a Log or a Config Loses Digits, and the Shortest Text That Does Not

questions.question: A run is logged with std::cout << value and the log is used to replay it. What goes wrong?
options: A stream writes six significant digits, so the number that is read back is a different one
questions.explanation: Of 20000 readings, 0 read back exactly through a stream.

questions.question: How many of 20000 readings of mixed size read back exactly after std::to_string, and after shortest_text?
options: 5627 and 20000: to_string writes large numbers in full, so some survive
questions.explanation: Six digits through a stream gave 0.

questions.question: What does std::to_string(3.5e-9) give?
options: 0.000000: it always writes six places after the point
questions.explanation: A time step that small is read back as zero.

questions.question: How does shortest_text find the shortest text?
options: It tries 1 significant digit, then 2, up to 17, and stops at the first text that reads back as the same double
questions.explanation: Readings to two decimal places averaged 5.8 characters against 15.7 at 17 digits.

questions.question: 0.1 + 0.2 and 0.3 are different doubles. How does each look in a six digit log, and in shortest_text?
options: Both 0.3 in a log, and 0.30000000000000004 and 0.3 in shortest_text
questions.explanation: A log with six digits cannot say they differ.

questions.question: Why does parse_number refuse nan, inf and 1e999 as well as 1.5x?
options: strtod accepts those words and overflow as numbers, and a configuration never means them, so they would break a division later
questions.explanation: All ten bad texts were refused and each left the output alone.
